title: 3-Read Friday #128
author: Craig Barton
summary: This issue of Craig Barton's weekly 3-Read Friday curates three blog posts with his own editorial framing. The first, by Mark Solomons, argues that improving initial teacher training reaches only a fraction of the profession and slowly, so the bigger gain is better professional learning for teachers already in schools. The second, by Ammar Merhbi, unpacks a large coaching study with nearly 1,000 coaches and about 6,000 mentees at $20 million a year that produced no gain in retention or achievement, and Barton agrees implementation is the key. The third, by Samantha Lippert, shows how multi-digit subtraction with regrouping hides prerequisite skills that experts no longer notice and breaks it into sequenced atoms. The mix is dominated by teacher training and professional development, so the issue sits in Practice & Culture, with the subtraction piece as a maths-teaching coda. Barton's contribution is the selection and his short verdicts on each piece.
points: Solomons argues that the teachers already in schools are the larger lever for improvement than initial teacher training, provided their professional learning changes shape.
Merhbi's account of a heavily funded coaching program with null results is a warning for anyone scaling professional development.
Barton believes coaching has real potential but that implementation details decide whether it works.
Lippert's atomised subtraction sequence is offered as a view into a teacher's planning process and the hidden prerequisites of familiar algorithms.

Ammar unpacks a study of a coaching programme with nearly 1,000 coaches, over 6,000 mentees and $20 million a year behind it. It made no difference to retention or achievement.

She breaks it into carefully sequenced atoms, each taught explicitly before the algorithm ever appears.
